items.title: How iFood scales coding agents across 15,000 repositories
items.story_key: story|title:how ifood scales coding agents across 15 000 repositories
items.content_excerpt: The Remote Agents Platform turned engineering tasks into API calls: teams delegate the work, execution takes place in a remote sandbox, and the result comes back as a merge request. In the internal security platform, the number of vulnerabilities fixed more than doubled. iFood maintains more than 15,000 code repositories. Each periodically needs specific tasks performed: validating code to ensure it meets internal standards, fixing vulnerable dependencies, or running an analysis. None of these tasks is difficult on its own. The challenge comes when those tasks multiply. “Solving this for one repository is easy. The challenge is solving it at scale,” says Victor Coelho, Senior Software Engineer at iFood. “The Remote Agents Platform is designed to make it possible to solve this at scale across all 15,000 repositories.” Before the platform, each team tackled the problem in its own way—and they all ran into the same obstacle. “Before, we had fragmented solutions. Imagine several teams at iFood trying to solve different problems, but without this layer, this agentic runtime, available to them. In the end, those solutions always ran into the same problem.” What was missing wasn’t intelligence or a use case. It was execution infrastructure. A dedicated runtime . The team describes the Remote Agents Platform as an API that launches a remote agentic coding task. The cycle has three steps: the user submits a prompt and environment requirements through a REST call; the platform processes the task on a dedicated remote runner inside an isolated sandbox; and the result is retrieved later. “The platform’s entry point, its interface, is a simple REST API. Users can use this API to create the runs they need. Internally, we handle and manage the entire lifecycle and delegate execution to isolated sandboxes,” he explains. Task progress can be monitored in real time. The runner’s internal design alternates between two different types of steps—and that combination makes the overall workflow predictable. Deterministic steps bookend the workflow: cloning the repository, importing the skills the agent can use, and setting up the working branch at the start; publishing the merge request and making the generated artifacts available at the end. In between is the agentic execution itself, running GPT‑5.6 Luna inside the sandbox. “It’s a combination of those two things: deterministic steps and agentic execution within the workflow.” The sandbox runs Ubuntu and includes the toolchains

items.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI
items.summary:
At QCon San Francisco 2026, OpenAI's Brian Yang described building the ChatGPT ads product with Codex agents and no human-written code. He outlined layered testing, sandboxes, and batched pull request reviews, and noted failure modes such as code "slop" and unsafe agent actions. He advised gradual adoption and framed engineers as managers of agents.

By Daniel Curtis

items.title: Learn the Effects, Not the Examples: Implicit ICL via Attention Patching
items.summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables language models to adapt to new tasks from demonstrations, but repeatedly including multiple examples increases context length and inference cost. Many existing implicit ICL methods encode demonstrations as fixed vectors, limiting adaptation of the intervention to individual queries and token positions. We propose Attention-Patching, an implicit ICL method that models contextual changes in self-attention outputs through task-specific updates to attention output projections. Using query-answer pairs processed with and without a fixed demonstration set, Attention-Patching fits layer-wise affine transformations from non-contextual attention representations to the demonstration-induced output changes. Across 12 classification benchmarks and four model families, Attention-Patching achieves higher average accuracy than the evaluated implicit ICL baselines while maintaining performance comparable to explicit ICL at near zero-shot inference cost. Further experiments on diverse generation tasks demonstrate its applicability to autoregressive multi-token generation.

items.title: Announcing vLLM-GR: Efficient Inference for Generative Recommendation
items.summary: vLLM-GR extends vLLM to serve generative recommendation models with accelerator-side beam search, catalog constraints, and shared KV caching across candidate paths.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:announcing vllm gr efficient inference for generative recommendation
items.content_excerpt: Today we’re introducing vLLM-GR , an open-source inference and serving framework built on vLLM for generative recommendation models. Consider a video feed. Given a viewer’s history, a model such as OneRec can generate a semantic ID (SID) for a video the viewer might watch next. To assemble a feed, the application needs a set of candidates. vLLM-GR extends vLLM’s model execution and paged key-value (KV) cache with beam search that explores multiple candidate IDs in one request. The overview shows how recommendation models generate item IDs or score supplied candidates. The OneRec-1.7B example below follows the generation path, from a viewer’s history to 128 candidate SIDs. A recommendation service has to turn a long interaction history into a set of candidates within a single request’s latency budget. Generating each item ID may take only a few tokens, yet the engine must explore many paths and return items the application can serve. vLLM-GR builds its recommendation search into the vLLM engine. vLLM supplies the scheduler, model execution, and paged KV cache. vLLM-GR adds a beam session that spans the whole search and keeps track of how candidate paths branch. EngineCore owns each beam session from admission to completion. The scheduler dispatches prefill and decode stages to a worker. At each stage, the model runner scores the next token and beam selection records the score and parent of each surviving path. The next decode uses those parent indices to read the right KV state. One request returns two candidates with beam widths of 2 → 3 → 2. The catalog filters out A1 · B1 because no item starts with that prefix. A full-vocabulary search skips this filter. The SIDs and scores are illustrative. In the prefill–decode–decode (PDD) pipeline, the scheduler admits a BeamSearch() request and dispatches its prefill stage to the worker. Prefill scores the first SID component while the host prepares decode 1. During decode 1, the host prepares decode 2. The second decode inherits the selected parents’ suffix KV and completes two SIDs. Green marks the component selected at each stage. The benchmarks measure P99 latency to show how beam width and batch size affect tail latency for generative recommendation. The two overview charts hold the input length at 1,024 tokens and compare beam widths of 256 and 128 at batch sizes 1, 4, and 8 across four NVIDIA GPUs and two Ascend NPUs. items.title: CocoonBench: Can Multilingual Search Agents Escape Language Information Cocoons?
items.summary: Multilingual search agents can access the global Web, yet may remain trapped in a language environment with insufficient evidence; we refer to this failure as a language information cocoon. However, existing search benchmarks largely operate within a single language, especially English, overlooking entity connections across multiple languages. We introduce CocoonBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether multilingual search agents can escape such language information cocoons. CocoonBench mines answer-centered relational paths from a frozen Wikidata-derived graph and selects clue sets that are individually necessary and jointly identify a unique answer. Using language-specific entity names, it records each task's minimum language cover, removes direct identifiers, and renders each task as matched prompts in three languages together with its construction certificate and provenance. Across 10 state-of-the-art models, mean accuracy on CocoonBench ranges from 33.8% (DeepSeek-V4-Flash) to 69.7% (Claude-Opus-4.8), leaving even the strongest system below 70%. The same construction certificates support path-aligned trajectory analysis, enabling diagnosis of model failures in language routing, evidence-path recovery, and answer use. The result shows that escaping a language cocoon requires more than switching languages: successful cross-lingual search depends on both covering the correct languages and connecting the evidence found across them.

items.title: RUIBench: What Makes a Good Robot-Use Interface?
items.summary: Foundation models can reason about complex physical tasks, yet translating this intelligence into reliable robot execution remains challenging. We argue that a critical, often overlooked factor is the robot-use interface (RUI), which determines how agents express and execute physical actions. To systematically study its impact, we introduce RUIBench, comprising 30 manipulation tasks across five suites spanning world knowledge, in-context learning, discovery, dynamic interaction, and contact-rich manipulation. We further develop RUIKit, a unified framework that crosses six action abstractions with two interaction forms, yielding 13 interfaces under shared perception and control. In simulation, changing only the RUI shifts a frontier agent's success rate from 45% to 81%, and that of a fine-tuned 4B model from 13% to 47%. Our analysis reveals that effective interfaces reduce unnecessary decisions while preserving essential feedback, with their benefits shaped by agent behavior and physical uncertainty. We further uncover a verification gap, where agents frequently declare success despite observable failures, revealing the need for task-level verification beyond individual actions. Together, these findings establish RUI design as a critical factor in embodied agent reliability.

items.title: Built for trust and control: Powering the next wave of AI agents across Google Workspace and Google Cloud
items.summary:
For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it.

That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path. 

Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence.

Purpose-built interfaces: Workspace MCP servers, Workspace CLI, and Cloud Agent Gateway

To help developers build reliable agents faster without forcing security teams to compromise, we are bringing agent-native interfaces to Workspace and Google Cloud:

  • Workspace MCP servers: Now generally available, dedicated remote servers for Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat, and Tasks. Builders get one standard interface with built-in permission and DLP checks, and native human-in-the-loop (HITL) confirmations for sensitive actions. They also reject non-agent OAuth clients and work with Model Armor, Google Cloud’s prompt-injection screening service.

  • Workspace CLI: Now generally available for local agents, terminal workflows, and automation, providing structured JSON outputs and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services.

  • Google Cloud Agent Gateway: A protocol-native gateway for LLM, MCP, and Agent2Agent (A2A) traffic on Google Cloud. It verifies Agent Identities against Agent Registry, enforces IAM policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor.

Together, these interfaces give AI agents open, protocol-native paths built on standards like MCP and A2A. Permissions, confirmations, prompt screening, and audit logging happen automatically, while traditional apps continue to run on existing REST APIs.

Consistent controls across every agent workflow

Those interfaces sit on a unified security model across Workspace and Google Cloud, with core controls shipping today:

  1. Policy checks on every request: Under our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum, AI agents must use Workspace MCP servers or the Workspace CLI rather than existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins on February 1, 2027, giving builders time to transition. Every call is checked against your organization’s Workspace permissions, DLP rules, and classification labels. On Google Cloud, Agent Gateway enforces IAM and default-deny outbound rules at the protocol layer and routes custom checks through Service Extensions to Identity-Aware Proxy, your own policy engine, or third-party security tools.

  2. Separate agent identities and limits: Admins and users need to tell an AI agent apart from a traditional app or a person, and cap what it can do. Agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs, paired with least-privilege scopes, time-limited approvals (coming soon), and usage quotas (billing begins on April 1, 2027). On Google Cloud, agents receive their own Agent Identity in Agent Registry with no shared or long-lived keys, bounded by IAM policies and organization, folder, and project quotas. Those identities can also carry user-delegated authorization into Workspace when accessing mail or files.

  3. People stay in charge of high-impact actions: Routine work like creating drafts or summarizing documents runs autonomously, while critical changes require a person to sign off. In Workspace, MCP servers and the CLI enforce explicit user confirmation before agents send email, change Drive sharing permissions, or make bulk edits. On Google Cloud, policy can require multi-factor authentication or human approval before reading sensitive Cloud Storage buckets, changing IAM permissions, or modifying production infrastructure.

  4. Clear visibility and revocation: A one-time consent screen is not enough when agents run continuously. Workspace administrators can view, audit, and revoke AI agents in the admin console, and users will soon be able to view agent activity and revoke access to their emails and files. On Google Cloud, Security Command Center, Agent Observability, Cloud Audit Logs, and Wiz surface unusual behavior. Revoking a Cloud Agent Identity or OAuth grant stops access immediately.

  5. Boundaries for your most sensitive data: Coming soon in Workspace, AI access restrictions extend Workspace DLP and client-side encryption protections to agents. This will allow admins and users to block agents from accessing messages in Gmail and specific files and folders in Drive. On Google Cloud, VPC Service Controls, Principal Access Boundaries, and Context-Aware Access keep sensitive data inside designated perimeters and verified devices.

  6. Strict rules on your data afterward: Our new Workspace AI Tools Addendum sets clear boundaries for AI tools using Workspace APIs. It does not allow permanent raw storage, model training, extended retention of derived data, or API scraping. Derived and user data are removed within a defined window and when a user disconnects. On Google Cloud, Sensitive Data Protection masks sensitive fields before data leaves, and customer-managed or external encryption keys let you cut off access to Cloud agent memory stores immediately.

Getting started

  • Workspace developers: Start building with the Workspace MCP and CLI configuration guide, implement user confirmations via MCP and prompt-injection protection such as Model Armor, and review the Workspace AI Tools Addendum.

  • Workspace administrators: Review connected apps and agents, configure DLP policies for your users, and monitor OAuth activity logs in the admin console.

  • Google Cloud customers: Register Agent Identities in Agent Registry, place Agent Gateway and Model Armor in front of agents and MCP servers, configure MFA or human approval for sensitive actions, and review IAM, VPC Service Controls, and quota limits.

With Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI generally available alongside Google Cloud’s agent protections, developers have an open, modern platform to build on. Organizations get the visibility and control to scale AI agents with confidence.

items.story_key: story|title:data modeling best practices for an agentic cdp part 1 the data foundation
items.content_excerpt: A customer saved a jacket to their wishlist on your site 9 days ago. This morning its price dropped 30%. Should you let them know? That depends on your goal. If you want first-time buyers to come back for a second purchase, the alert could help. If you're growing lifetime value and this customer usually pays full price, the discount may cost more than it earns. Whatever the goal, an agent needs six answers about this one person before it makes the call (Figure 1). Figure 1. The goal frames one price-drop decision, and the decision needs answers from six kinds of data. If you're getting customer data ready for an Agentic CDP, start here. At Databricks, we work with many brands on this, and the data model is usually the hardest part. This post is for the data architect who designs the stack that marketers, and now agents, build on. This is Part 1 of a two-part series. Part 1: the modeling steps, from raw data to omnichannel activation. Part 2: mapping B2C and B2B datasets, attributes and use cases onto the model. An Agentic CDP needs everything a traditional CDP needs: the right sources, clean data, one identity per customer and golden profiles marketers trust. If you've built a CDP before, that work carries over. If you haven't, it's the place to start. What changes is who does the work and how fast the data has to be right. Agents take on more of the work, such as matching records and drafting audiences, while people choose the sources, review the matches and approve what goes out. And because an agent decides for one person in seconds, a gap in the data turns into a bad decision just as fast. Databricks built CustomerLake around the same idea. Data teams can define trusted datasets and models once through Databricks and Unity Catalog. Marketers can then use purpose-built interfaces to ask questions, build segments, and activate audiences faster without working around IT or exporting data into unmanaged tools. Here's the flow we recommend. It's a medallion architecture with one important rule: identity resolution runs after silver, and the canonical ID it creates becomes the join key for gold. You build the layers with Spark Declarative Pipelines , keep them on schedule with Lakeflow Jobs and govern every layer in Unity Catalog . Figure 2. items.title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains
items.summary: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

items.title: SayDo: Benchmarking the Safety of Frontier Models from Chat to Closed-Loop Robot Control
items.summary: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level robot controllers, yet their safety is evaluated almost entirely in text. We introduce SayDo, a benchmark that assesses the propensity of frontier models to cause harm in embodied contexts. SayDo comprises eleven laboratory and household tasks that pair a benign instruction with a hazard latent in the scene. Tasks are implemented in six settings along an embodiment gradient, from chat questions about an imagined robot to closed-loop control of a simulated robot arm. Benign controls, safe-alternative variants and scripted operator pushback complement each task. Across six open- and closed-weight VLMs and 11,480 episodes, hazardous-action rates rise from 14% in chat to 47% in the simulator, and from 2% to 80% for the most affected model. The increase is largely driven by open-weight models. We find that models flag hazards before acting in 73% of unsafe episodes and give way to pushback about twice as often when controlling robots as in chat. The safest models also show signs of overcaution on benign controls. Safety evaluations run in text therefore do not predict the safety behavior of the same models when used as robot controllers.

items.title: Keeping Agents Fast: High-Interactivity Decode with FlyDSL MonoKernels in vLLM
items.summary: How FlyDSL MonoKernels keep agents responsive with high-interactivity decode in vLLM on AMD Instinct GPUs, using model-specific fusion, data-ready handoffs, and specialized-decode integration.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:keeping agents fast high interactivity decode with flydsl monokernels in vllm
items.content_excerpt: Interactive LLM applications depend on low decode latency. A coding agent must finish generating its current action before it can call the next tool, so decode sits on the task’s critical path. Serving these workloads at low concurrency prioritizes per-user responsiveness over aggregate throughput. A decode step executes a chain of GPU kernels for operations such as projections, attention, and expert computation. At small batch sizes, many of these kernels do only a little work, yet each still incurs GPU-side dispatch, startup, and completion costs. A dependent kernel cannot proceed until its inputs are ready, so whole-kernel boundaries also limit overlap. Repeated across a long chain, these costs can account for a substantial part of decode latency, while the small amount of parallel work leaves GPU capacity unused. HIP graphs reduce CPU launch overhead, but do not eliminate these GPU-side costs. Figure 1 illustrates the repeated stages; widths and gaps are schematic, not measured durations or an overhead breakdown. This post explores how MonoKernels written in FlyDSL reduce decode latency in vLLM for interactive LLM serving on AMD Instinct GPUs. We explain the approach and its integration with vLLM, then examine performance and accuracy. A MonoKernel combines multiple dependent operator stages inside a single GPU kernel launch, using an explicitly designed schedule rather than a separate launch at every operator boundary. Here, mono means a single kernel execution boundary, not an entire model in one kernel. A model’s mono-decode path can contain several MonoKernels, and a decoder layer does not have to map to exactly one launch. The goal is not just to make individual operators faster, but to shorten the waits between them. Inspired by TileRT , the implementations discussed here use a persistent launch : a fixed grid of GPU thread blocks works through multiple stages. A thread block is a group of GPU threads executing together; it can continue with subsequent work once the required dependencies are satisfied. Both paths in Figure 2 can be replayed under HIP graphs. The difference is between multiple independent kernels and an author-designed persistent schedule within a launch. Some whole-kernel boundaries become finer-grained handoffs between portions of the computation. items.title: How to build a knowledge factory for AI agents
items.summary: The knowledge factory is how LangChain keeps its agents' company knowledge current: agents flag what's missing, and a curator agent fixes it in the background.
items.story_key: story|title:how to build a knowledge factory for ai agents
items.content_excerpt: In order to make AI work for your company, the missing bit is not better models, it’s not just more context - it’s better knowledge. It’s knowledge of how your company works, what standards for operating you have in place, where data is stored and how it’s accessed. Your most efficient employees have this knowledge in their head. They know who to talk to, where to go to answer questions, why you do things in a particular way. That knowledge is often tacit, implicit, scattered - sometimes present only in their head, sometimes scattered across a variety of documents. In order to make AI work for your company, you need to collect, curate, and maintain a representation of that knowledge to pass to agents. The system that helps you do that is what we’re calling a knowledge factory. We’ve built this at LangChain in a few ways. Our internal GTM and content studio agents are powered by a knowledge factory. LangSmith Engine (our agent that runs over traces and suggests fixes) maintains a knowledge factory per agent as well. This blog shares our learnings. Knowledge is the reusable understanding we maintain so it can do that task correctly: what a metric means, which source to trust, or how we handle a particular situation. Sometimes written down, often not. A knowledge factory turns scattered documents and experience into knowledge that can become context for future work. So knowledge is a form of context that the agent will get, but it’s often not (and shouldn’t be) the only context the agent gets. Other types of context you already ingest/store reliably, and that can just be provided directly to the agent (see the section on quickly changing data below). The idea of software factories has risen sharply over the past year and a half. The idea is that rather than having your best engineers actually build software, they should build the factory (the systems) to help everyone at the company build software more efficiently. The actual building of the software can be done by agents. General knowledge work is now following a similar path. Agents are good enough to make presentations, launch videos, do outbound. You should be leveraging them as much as possible for those tasks. But in order for them to accomplish those tasks they need all that tacit, implicit, scattered knowledge. That is where you should devote resources. You need to build that knowledge, and more importantly a factory to collect, curate and maintain that knowledge. That is what will let you outsource m

items.title: claude-code v2.1.331
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Code Mode support in terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS
  • Added oidc.groups_jsonpath to the Claude apps gateway, to read groups from the matching entries of a list of objects with a small subset of JSONPath (RFC 9535)
  • Added an API connectivity section to claude doctor that reports whether the API can be reached, with the HTTP status or the error, or says why it wasn't tested
  • Added a notice when tap-mode voice dictation stops by itself, after 15 seconds without recognized speech or at its 2-minute limit
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_RESPONSE_COMPRESSION to ask for uncompressed model responses behind a proxy that cuts compressed ones off; not advised yet for self-hosted runners or Remote Control
  • Added CLAUDE_GATEWAY_IDP_CONNECT_BY_HOSTNAME=1 for Claude apps gateways: with oidc.use_proxy: true, sign-in requests hand the proxy an https IdP's hostname even with NO_PROXY set
  • Added gen_ai.usage.*, gen_ai.response.model and gen_ai.operation.name to claude_code.llm_request trace spans; gen_ai.usage.input_tokens includes prompt cache tokens
  • Added optionalDependencies to plugin manifests: plugins that install with the plugin listing them and can be disabled or uninstalled on their own
  • Fixed MCP tool calls hanging for up to 30 minutes on some malformed replies from a local or WebSocket server
  • Fixed PushNotification telling a headless run, such as a scheduled one, that the terminal was active in its first minute, instead of saying whether a mobile push was requested
  • Fixed /install-github-app skipping the repository step after setup warnings when no repository was found, and Esc not going back from its workflow list and sign-in steps
  • Fixed one-line tool results cut with no ellipsis in narrow windows, Markdown stars in the Auto mode tab of /permissions, and a hook's reason to stop a forked skill showing twice
  • Fixed /diff hiding its key hints and not selecting files in windows of 24 to 26 rows, and leaving out files added with git add -N in a repository with no commits
  • Fixed the first-run theme list showing too few themes in short windows, and /usage and other tall screens coming out garbled there
  • Fixed /bug in fullscreen hiding its Yes and No answers behind a long report, and Yes staying out of view in very short windows
  • Fixed /compact and auto-compact sometimes losing part of the conversation summary when the summary quoted certain XML tags
  • Fixed Claude not being told when permission rules on the Agent tool dropped its queued message to a subagent that had already ended
  • Fixed a Remote Control message sometimes showing above the reply that was finishing when it was sent
  • Fixed Stop hooks that read the transcript missing the last reply in Claude Desktop; SubagentStop hooks now wait for it too
  • Fixed turns and subagents failing in cloud sessions, or timing out on long replies elsewhere, when a reply went silent while Claude was still thinking; Claude Code now tries the request once more
  • Fixed Esc and Stop waiting about a minute or more when the contents of a cloud or network file that Claude is reading stall
  • Fixed Code Mode sessions resumed with --resume or --continue in another permission mode losing thinking and the prompt cache; one begun in a mode that asks keeps that mode's limits on scripts
  • Fixed Code Mode sending a request about every second when a ! or slash command was typed while a script was running
  • Fixed an interrupted or failed plugin update leaving a partial plugin folder that later loaded with skills or other components missing (#102186)
  • Windows: Fixed file writes on FAT32 and exFAT drives asking for permission every time in some plugin sessions
  • Fixed Claude failing to read a notebook that has a null output or an error output with no traceback
  • Fixed a rewind deleting files after a restore had failed
  • Fixed auto mode sometimes refusing Claude's call to stop a /loop, which left the next wake-up to fire
  • Fixed a Workflow agent's background shells and MCP servers sometimes being left running after it handed back its report
  • Windows: Fixed /desktop downloading the older Claude Desktop installer, and asking for an update when an older install's folder was left behind
  • Fixed claude plugin install, marketplace add and similar commands hanging with no output when managed settings needed an approval that could not be asked for
  • Fixed a permission rule on a subagent's model, such as Agent(model:*), blocking Claude's follow-up message to a subagent started on this version with no model named
  • Fixed PermissionRequest hooks not saving Skill(name:*) allow rules outside local settings
  • Fixed "Ask your admin" asking to raise your own limit when your team's pooled group budget blocked you, and saying "Request sent" when an admin had approved your request in the last few minutes
  • Fixed Code Mode losing the middle of a long script output; Claude now gets a path to the uncut text (#111373)
  • Fixed hold-to-talk dictation stopping early and losing words when Claude Code was busy
  • Fixed Code Mode with --bare not telling Claude what its scripts can call
  • Fixed a crash when a custom API endpoint returned a tool call with no tool name; the call now fails with an error and the session continues
  • Windows: Fixed a possible crash when the machine is almost out of memory
  • Fixed the CLI freezing on some replies, and quoted text sometimes going missing or showing twice
  • Windows: Fixed Claude Code refusing to start when managed settings in the registry contain non-ASCII characters such as Japanese (#93280)
  • Windows: Fixed Remote Control clients showing no steps for a new subagent
  • Fixed @-mentions written as @file#10-12 attaching the whole file instead of those lines
  • Fixed Claude misreading a pasted artifact invitation link; it now asks you to accept the invitation and paste the artifact's own link
  • Fixed sandboxed Bash commands sometimes failing to start on a full temp disk, for sandboxes whose file rules keep commands out of the temp directory
  • Improved typing speed in screen reader mode, most of all in long sessions
  • Improved start-up time: a session started soon after another no longer waits for the model list, and one outside a git repository without .claude/settings.local.json no longer waits on git
  • Windows: Improved the speed of the first Bash command in a session on machines with no custom shell start-up files
  • Improved the plugin auto-update notice to name plugins it newly installs as dependencies, separately from updated plugins
  • Improved Code Mode tool search to show more of an MCP tool's description, with its limits, formats and defaults
  • Improved the Console sign-in link shown by /login and claude auth login --console: it is now much shorter
  • Improved Claude's list of your artifacts: it now marks web pages, so Claude is less likely to try opening one with the Claude Docs connector
  • Improved the folder trust prompts in short terminals: fullscreen /cd and /add-dir show their choices in fewer rows, and the prompt at launch keeps the folder path in view when it has many warnings
  • Changed the questions for stopping auto-connect in /ide and for /clear, /compact or /rewind in a subagent's view to list Yes first; they still start on No, so Down then Enter now answers No
  • Changed what a PermissionDenied hook's retry: true tells Claude: make the refused call again only if you asked for that call
  • Changed in a future release, on or after November 30, 2026: plugin marketplaces in managed extraKnownMarketplaces will auto-update by default. To opt one out, set "autoUpdate": false on its entry
  • Windows: Changed start-up with managed settings in the registry: check them before upgrading, as an HKLM policy outranks managed-settings.json and a broken value can stop the start
  • [VSCode] Added a warning and a link to the revoke page when you log out and the request to revoke your claude.ai login isn't confirmed
  • [VSCode] Added a notice before sending a very large selection or attached text file, and advice under "Prompt is too long" that names the large part and what to do next
  • [VSCode] Added "Add Cell to Chat" to the notebook cell menu, which attaches a cell with its outputs or error
  • [VSCode] Added "Fix with Claude Code" as a quick fix for errors and warnings and to failed tests in the test peek and the Test Results view, which puts the problem into the chat box
  • [VSCode] Added "Add to Chat" to the right-click menu of changed files in the Source Control view
  • [VSCode] Added "Resolve Merge Conflicts" to the editor title of a file with merge conflicts and to the Merge Changes group in Source Control
  • [VSCode] Fixed raw tags for selected code under a reworded prompt, the mode button flashing Manual, the slash menu hiding its highlighted row, a broken sign-in image, and a blinking Accept/Reject bar
  • [VSCode] Fixed a forked conversation overwriting the original conversation's plan file; a fork or rewind that can't copy the plan now shows a warning
  • [VSCode] Fixed voice dictation saying no speech was recognized when its connection closed or never opened; it now says the connection was lost or couldn't connect
  • [VSCode] Fixed an unsent side question being lost when its panel closes
  • [VSCode] Fixed Escape stopping Claude after renaming a session, and typing going nowhere after closing the session history with Escape
  • [VSCode] Fixed Rename, Mark as Unread and Add to Group saying "still connecting" on a tab that resumed a session from its history
  • [VSCode] Fixed wide tables and long paths cut off, long errors hiding their close button, errors out of view in the Add MCP server form and Chrome dialog, and plugin pictures ignoring the editor theme
  • [VSCode] Fixed later prompts and the message box covering the Rewind code dialog, and focus jumping from "Never mind" to "Rewind" when it finishes checking files
  • [VSCode] Fixed the command menu keeping an earlier match highlighted while you type more in its filter, so Enter could run the wrong row
  • [VSCode] Fixed the @ menu showing "No files found" before its first search results arrived, or when it couldn't search all files of a very large workspace, which it now says
  • [VSCode] Fixed Escape stopping Claude at a Remove or Delete confirmation in MCP, Hooks and Memory dialogs, on a side question panel's button or link, and on the Bookmarks button with its panel open
  • [VSCode] Fixed empty boxes showing instead of the + and − signs in diffs (#73069)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat no longer following Claude's reply after the panel was resized, or hidden and shown again
  • [VSCode] Fixed a chat left in bypass permissions mode reopening in Auto mode instead of your initial permission mode when settings disable bypass
  • [VSCode] Fixed the chat panel freezing on some CSS code blocks and diffs
  • [VSCode] Fixed the context usage indicator disappearing after an API error, "Prompt is too long", or a slash command
  • [VSCode] Fixed a message queued behind a queued /clear being lost
  • [VSCode] Fixed Manage Plugins losing its search box or showing no message when a search has no match, and not saying that the list of available plugins failed to load
  • [VSCode] Fixed proposed changes to notebooks and files with a custom editor opening in a tab with no Accept or Reject that stayed open after the answer
  • [VSCode] Fixed the spend limit message telling Team and Enterprise members to run /usage-credits, which can't send a request to their admin from the panel
  • [VSCode] Fixed a written message being wiped by Tab on a command in the "/" button's menu or by a click on an onboarding suggestion
  • [VSCode] Fixed Claude continuing to edit files after you rewind code while it is working
  • [VSCode] Fixed typed text being lost after /tasks, /copy, /export, a skipped /feedback, or /plan while already in plan mode
  • [VSCode] Fixed the question card dropping a typed "Other" answer on Ctrl/Cmd+Enter, and sending the word "Other" when nothing was typed
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing "Something went wrong" for a conversation in which a gateway sent a tool call with no name
  • [VSCode] Fixed unsaved changes being missed, and Claude's edit being overwritten by the next save, in a folder opened through a symlink
  • [VSCode] Fixed @-mentions attaching nothing, or another file of the same name, after Claude changed folders with cd
  • [VSCode] Fixed the arrow keys replacing typed text with an old prompt while selecting, and dropping edits to a recalled prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed an @-mention added while a permission prompt was open being lost
  • [VSCode] Fixed shortcuts such as Ctrl+1, Alt+1 or Ctrl+Space answering an open dialog, which could restore files in the rewind confirmation or switch the git branch
  • [VSCode] Fixed prompts that start with a file path or code comment being sent without the selected code and having no fork or rewind menu
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links in the chat ignoring your editor associations for files in the workspace, except notebooks (#81482)
  • [VSCode] Fixed selected lines staying attached to your next message after their file's tab was closed
  • [VSCode] Fixed new sessions starting in Edit automatically after pressing Shift+Tab through it to reach Plan mode
  • [VSCode] Fixed an edited command on the permission prompt running without the line breaks that were typed or pasted into it
  • [VSCode] Fixed a newly opened Claude tab not focusing its message box, or taking the keyboard late from the terminal or command palette and sending the typed text as a prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed Alt+K line ranges such as @app.ts#5-10 sending the whole file, or its first 2,000 lines, instead of the selected lines
  • [VSCode] Fixed diff tabs opening out of order when several subagents wait for approval, and a later edit to the same file cancelling an earlier one
  • [VSCode] Fixed Enter rewriting a message or running a menu action when a /word such as the path /api stands beside other text, and running a typed slash command without its arguments
  • [VSCode] Fixed Electron apps and extension tests failing to start from Claude, a hook or an MCP server; a wrapper, hook or server that runs VS Code as Node must now set ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE=1
  • [VSCode] Fixed Claude not being told when you reject part of a proposed edit or change it in the diff view before accepting
  • [VSCode] Fixed Escape on a permission prompt sending a half-typed instruction to Claude instead of cancelling
  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+J and Ctrl+O in the chat also opening VS Code's terminal or Open File dialog on Windows and Linux
  • [VSCode] Fixed the @ menu inserting the wrong file on a quick Tab or Enter, and Enter not sending a prompt that ends in an @word with no matching file
  • [VSCode] Fixed new Claude tabs staying blank and the side bar failing to load after closing a tab while Claude was still starting
  • [VSCode] Fixed a quick double click in the panel pressing a button or row that appeared after the first click, or starting a second compaction from the context usage circle
  • [VSCode] Fixed switching models failing with "Settings file is not valid JSON" when settings.json is empty or starts with a byte order mark
  • [VSCode] Fixed memory growing with each fork or rewind of a long conversation until the window was reloaded
  • [VSCode] Fixed plan comments not showing on the plan approval card in Focus view
  • [VSCode] Fixed file links without a line number moving the cursor of an open file to line 1
  • [VSCode] Fixed a missing notification when a conversation running behind another one in the same panel needs a permission or an answer
  • [VSCode] Fixed Manage Plugins not loading when Claude Code is slow to start or fails to start, so a plugin that blocks startup can be turned off
  • [VSCode] Fixed proposed diffs showing and saving garbled non-ASCII text when files.encoding is not UTF-8
  • [VSCode] Fixed approved edits and writes saving right-to-left marks as literal \u200F escapes on lines with Hebrew, Arabic or Persian text
  • [VSCode] Fixed a model pick being ignored for the next message when Claude's process had ended or was still starting
  • [VSCode] Fixed Rewind showing "No active session" after Claude's process had ended
  • [VSCode] Fixed typing @ leaving a helper process running per tab when no browser is connected, except when Claude in Chrome's service can't be reached
  • [VSCode] Fixed the session list opening every transcript at once, which stalled the editor's extensions and could leave sessions out in projects with many sessions
  • [VSCode] Improved the time to the first reply in a new folder when the Python extension is installed and the folder has no Python
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in screen to say when it opened because a request was refused
  • [VSCode] Improved the speed of opening, restoring and switching back to long conversations, most of all with many file edits or where git is slow
  • [VSCode] Improved responsiveness in long chats: smooth typing and large file writes while a reply streams, faster permission prompts, and far less freezing on send with accessibility support on
  • [VSCode] Improved startup and memory use: the panel and new chat tabs open faster, a first message in a new tab is answered sooner, and on Pro and Max plans the folder trust dialog comes up sooner
  • [VSCode] Improved speed in remote windows (SSH, WSL, containers): the panel starts, replies appear and sessions reopen faster
  • [VSCode] Improved the time to a response for the first message after a chat has been idle for a few minutes on a machine that is low on memory
  • [VSCode] Improved how fast chats start, open from history and come back after a restart on slow or antivirus-scanned disks
  • [VSCode] Improved how fast diffs appear in reopened conversations, and removed diff menu entries that did not work
  • [VSCode] Improved the @ file menu to list the files of open editor tabs first, the most recently used on top
  • [VSCode] Changed saving a proposed diff to accept it only after you click or type in its proposed (right) side; a notification says when a save is refused or a close with Save applies nothing
  • [VSCode] Changed diffs from a terminal session to open without moving keyboard focus, and beside a file with unsaved changes; to answer, click Accept or use the terminal
  • [VSCode] Changed permission cards to show only Yes and No when allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly is set and the card would offer an allow rule; key 2 on those cards now answers No
  • [VSCode] Changed a Claude tab to ignore Enter and show a notice when its Find box has lost the keyboard

items.title: Genie 4 is now available
items.content_excerpt: Explore a new Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers, featuring Genie 4, the Project Genie agent, and a community gallery. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command. items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
release_highlights: PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support
THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers
Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits
